title: Early-life inhalant allergen exposure, filaggrin genotype, and the development of sensitization from infancy to adolescence.
ehr_evidence: The Manchester Asthma and Allergy Study is an unselected birth cohort described in detail elsewhere. The source actually consisted of prospectively collected home dust samples, skin prick test results, genotyping data, and questionnaire responses.
summary: Longitudinal birth cohort study examining how early-life inhalant allergen exposure interacts with filaggrin (FLG) loss-of-function mutations to influence the development of allergic sensitization from infancy to age 16.
key_findings: Significant interaction between FLG mutations and Fel d 1 exposure on cat sensitization (OR, 1.36; 95% CI, 1.02-1.80; P = .035), with a greater effect in children with FLG mutations.
Increased risk of mite sensitization with Der p 1 exposure was consistently greater among children with FLG mutations, but the interaction did not reach statistical significance.

Significant interaction between FLG mutations and dog ownership on sensitization to any allergen (OR, 0.16; 95% CI, 0.03-0.86; P = .03), with significantly lower risk in children with FLG mutations exposed to a dog in infancy.
No significant interaction was found between FLG mutations and Can f 1 exposure on dog sensitization.
captured_features: Dust allergen concentrations (Der p 1, Fel d 1, Can f 1)
Demographic and confounding variables (sex, socioeconomic status, breast-feeding)
study_design: Population-based prospective birth cohort with longitudinal follow-up from infancy to age 16 years
population: 1051 children from the Manchester Asthma and Allergy Study observational cohort, followed from infancy to age 16 years (predominantly white)
exposure_domain: Early-life inhalant allergen exposure (house dust mite, cat, dog) and pet ownership
limitations: Exclusion of non-white participants due to FLG mutation prevalence
Reduced sample size due to missing dust samples and genotyping data
Inability to assess relative importance of exposure in infancy versus later childhood
Smaller sample size at age 1 year and in some subgroups
